Add priors to a stochastic frontier model

Source: R/add_priors.R
add_priors.Rd

Attaches the prior specification to a model object produced by create_sfmodel_exp or create_sfmodel_hn.

add_priors(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'sfmodel_exp'
add_priors(
  object,
  coef = list(mu = 0, v_i = 0.01),
  sigma = list(shape = 0.01, rate = 0.01),
  lambda = list(r_star = 0.75, shape = 1),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'sfmodel_hn'
add_priors(
  object,
  coef = list(mu = 0, v_i = 0.01),
  sigma = list(shape = 0.01, rate = 0.01),
  sigma_u = list(r_star = 0.75, shape = 2.5),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

an object of class "sfmodel_exp" or "sfmodel_hn".

...

unused, for compatibility with the generic.

coef

a named list of prior specifications for the frontier coefficients, with elements mu, the prior mean, and v_i, the prior precision. Scalars are expanded to a common mean and a diagonal precision matrix; a vector for mu and a matrix for v_i may be given instead.

sigma

a named list of prior specifications for the error precision, with elements shape and rate.

lambda

a named list of prior specifications for the rate of the exponential inefficiency distribution, with elements r_star, the prior median efficiency, and shape.

sigma_u

a named list of prior specifications for the scale of the half-normal inefficiency distribution, with elements r_star and shape.

Value

The model object with the element priors attached.

Details

The frontier coefficients receive a normal prior with mean mu and precision v_i, and the error precision \(\sigma_v^{-2}\) a gamma prior with the given shape and rate.

The inefficiency term is hard to elicit directly, so its prior is anchored on r_star, the efficiency score the researcher considers equally likely to be exceeded as not, a priori. How that anchor maps into a prior differs between the two models, which is why there is one method per class.

Because r_star is an efficiency, it fixes the scale of \(u\) in the units of the response. This is only meaningful if the response is on a logarithmic scale, where \(u\) is a proportional shortfall. A model fitted to output in levels will return efficiency scores that depend on the units the output happens to be measured in.

For the exponential model the mapping is exact. Placing a gamma prior of shape 1 and rate \(c = -\log(r^*)\) on the rate parameter \(\lambda\) implies the marginal prior density $$p(u) = \int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda u} c e^{-c\lambda} d\lambda = c / (u + c)^2,$$ whose median is exactly \(c\), so that the prior median of \(\exp(-u)\) is \(r^*\). This is the elicitation of van den Broeck, Koop, Osiewalski and Steel (1994), and the default shape of 1 corresponds to the two degrees of freedom they use.

For the half-normal model no such exact result is available, and the anchor is matched only in expectation: the prior mean of \(\sigma_u^2\) is set to the value that would place the median of \(u\) at \(-\log(r^*)\), namely \((-\log(r^*) / \Phi^{-1}(0.75))^2\). The shape must exceed one for that mean to exist, hence the higher default.

References

van den Broeck, J., Koop, G., Osiewalski, J., & Steel, M. F. J. (1994). Stochastic frontier models: A Bayesian perspective. Journal of Econometrics, 61(2), 273–303.

Examples

set.seed(1234)
d <- sim_sf(n = 200, beta = c(1, 0.5, 0.3), sigma_v = 0.2, par_u = 4)

model <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d,
                            iterations = 500, burnin = 200)
model <- add_priors(model, lambda = list(r_star = 0.85))
model$priors$rate_u
#> [1] 0.1625189
